strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored question: why deep vanilla GNNs may fail to train even though, in principle, sufficiently large weights could avoid forward oversmoothing. Reframing oversmoothing as an optimization-landscape phenomenon is useful and timely.

The main conceptual contribution, backward oversmoothing and its interaction with forward smoothing under nonlinear activations, is interesting. The paper distinguishes this from simple vanishing gradients and gives a GNN-specific contrast with MLPs.

The theoretical development is reasonably coherent: the paper states assumptions, derives rates for backward signal smoothing, connects output-layer stationarity to global near-stationarity, and provides appendix proofs for the main results.

The limitations section is honest about the scope: vanilla GNNs only, no skip connections or normalization, and no proposed mitigation method. I do not see material ethical concerns for this mainly theoretical work.
weaknesses: The applicability of the results is quite narrow. The analysis assumes symmetric bistochastic propagation, full-batch gradients, bounded/nonexpanding weight regimes, smooth activations with Lipschitz derivative, and often balanced/iid labels. These assumptions exclude many common GNN training settings and architectures, including standard ReLU-based models and typical normalized adjacency choices.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper argues this is the main reason deep GNNs are hard to train, but the empirical support is limited to toy CSBM figures and the theory only covers vanilla GNNs without common anti-oversmoothing mechanisms.

Reproducibility is weak: the manuscript says the code is available but leaves the URL blank, and the experimental figures lack enough detail on hyperparameters, initialization, optimizer, dataset parameters, and random variability to independently verify the empirical claims.

There are presentation and notation issues in important proof sections. For example, the appendix sometimes writes gradients with respect to H when the displayed quantity is a weight gradient, theorem/proof references appear inconsistent, and there are minor derivative/factor typos. These do not necessarily invalidate the results, but they make the proofs harder to audit.

The paper would benefit from stronger empirical validation on standard graph benchmarks and with controlled ablations showing that the predicted stationary behavior tracks depth, spectral expansion, activation smoothness, and graph spectral gap. Without this, significance is mostly theoretical and specialized.

The activation discussion is slightly misleading: the text says smoothed ReLU variants like softplus are included, but the stated condition |rho(x)| <= |x| is not satisfied by vanilla softplus at zero. This should be clarified or corrected.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and underexplored angle on oversmoothing: the role of backpropagated errors and their interaction with forward oversmoothing in deep GNN optimization.
The theoretical development is aimed at a real gap in the literature, namely why a vanilla deep GNN may fail to learn weights that avoid oversmoothing even when such weights exist.
The distinction between GNNs and MLPs is useful, and Proposition 2 is a good attempt to show that the identified mechanism is graph-specific rather than just another generic deep-network pathology.
The limitations section is reasonably honest: the authors acknowledge that the results do not cover skip connections, normalization, or other standard anti-oversmoothing mechanisms.
weaknesses: The central claims are much stronger than the evidence supports. The paper repeatedly argues that deep GNNs get stuck because the last layer trains and then the whole model becomes stationary, but the theorems only establish near-stationarity under restrictive spectral, depth, width/sample-size, label-distribution, and last-layer stationarity conditions. They do not prove that gradient descent reaches these regions, that the regions are attracting, or that this is the main practical cause of failed training.

The theory applies only to a narrow vanilla setting: symmetric bi-stochastic propagation matrices, full-batch training, largely all-node supervision, bounded spectral norms, smooth activations with Lipschitz derivatives, and no ReLU, residual connections, normalization, attention, sampling, or common GNN training machinery. This sharply limits significance for modern GNN practice.

The empirical support is very weak. The paper shows only small synthetic CSBM illustrations in Figures 1 and 2, apparently with one setup and no meaningful ablations, real graph benchmarks, comparison to anti-oversmoothing architectures, sensitivity to depth/initialization/activation, or validation that the theoretical quantities predict optimization failure in practice.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript says “the code is available at” but provides no visible URL, and the experimental details are insufficient to reproduce the figures: model widths, optimizer settings, learning rates, seeds, graph parameters, activation choice, initialization, and exact losses are not adequately specified in the main text.

The spurious-stationary-point result is not very convincing as evidence for practical failure. Corollary 2 relies on an existence construction with a degenerate high-loss region, but does not show that typical training enters such a region or that the construction explains the empirical behavior of realistic GNNs.

Several assumptions are presented as mild but are consequential. For example, excluding ReLU, requiring balanced or centered iid labels in parts of Theorem 3, and imposing strong depth and sample-size requirements are not minor technicalities; they change the scope of the result substantially.

The presentation has numerous rough edges and overclaims: missing code link, typographical issues, inconsistent theorem/proof references, and language such as “as soon as the last layer is trained” or “main reason why deep GNNs are hard to train” that is not justified by the formal results.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important theoretical gap: oversmoothing is usually treated as a forward representation phenomenon, while the optimization consequences of backward smoothing are less understood. The framing around backward oversmoothing and spurious near-stationary regions for deep GNNs is conceptually useful.

The main technical contribution is substantial. The paper extends gradient/backward oversmoothing analysis beyond the linear case by showing how forward smoothing makes the nonlinear backpropagation recursion effectively linear in middle layers, and then connects this to global near-stationarity once the last layer is trained.
The results are specific to GNNs rather than generic deep-network pathology: the MLP counterexample is a useful sanity check and helps clarify the mechanism.

The exposition is mostly clear, with helpful intuition after the formal statements. The limitations section is honest: the authors explicitly state that the results do not cover common anti-oversmoothing mechanisms such as residual connections and normalization.
The empirical figures are limited but well aligned with the theory, illustrating gradient collapse and the contrast between deep GNNs and MLPs on CSBM data.
weaknesses: The scope of the theory is quite restricted. Key assumptions include symmetric bi-stochastic propagation matrices, full-batch gradients, smooth activations with Lipschitz derivative, bounded spectral expansion, and in some results balanced or centered label distributions. These assumptions exclude many standard practical settings, including ReLU-like activations, common normalized adjacency choices, mini-batch/subgraph training, residual/normalization-based deep GNNs, and heterophilous or imbalanced tasks.

The paper does not propose or evaluate mitigation strategies. This is acceptable for a theory paper, but it limits significance: the work improves understanding more than it directly changes practice.

The empirical support is mainly illustrative. The experiments appear to be confined to CSBM-style synthetic data and simple GNN/MLP comparisons; there is no systematic evaluation across real graph benchmarks, propagation matrices, activations, depths, initialization scales, or architectures with common oversmoothing fixes.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript says code is available but the link is blank. Experimental details for the figures are also sparse, so reproducing the empirical claims would require guesswork.

Some central claims are phrased broadly, e.g. that deep GNNs get stuck because the last layer quickly reaches a stationary point, while the formal results establish this under specialized regimes and near-stationarity conditions. The manuscript should more consistently separate theorem-level conclusions from broader practical interpretation.

There are several presentation issues and minor notation inconsistencies/typos, including missing code URL, occasional grammatical errors, and possible confusion between gradients with respect to W and H in definitions/proof text. These do not undermine the main idea but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and relatively underexplored optimization-side mechanism for deep GNN failure: backward oversmoothing of backpropagated errors, and connects it to near-stationary points rather than merely to standard vanishing gradients.

The theoretical development is fairly coherent and GNN-specific. The distinction between forward oversmoothing, backward oversmoothing, and MLP behavior is useful, and Proposition 2 helps support the claim that the phenomenon is not just a generic deep-network pathology.

The paper is honest about scope: it does not claim to solve oversmoothing, explicitly restricts attention to vanilla message-passing GNNs, and discusses skip connections/normalization as important future work.
The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, with helpful proof sketches and appendices. The illustrative experiments align qualitatively with the theory across several datasets.
weaknesses: The main claims rely on restrictive assumptions that substantially limit significance: full-batch training, stochastic irreducible propagation matrices, bounded/non-expanding weights with s <= lambda^{-alpha}, smooth activations excluding ReLU, and vanilla GNNs without the residual/normalization mechanisms commonly used to train deep GNNs.

A key premise, forward oversmoothing for nonlinear non-symmetric stochastic P, is assumed rather than proved. The authors explicitly note this gap, but it weakens the reach of the central theorems because common GNN settings often use nonlinear activations and non-symmetric random-walk matrices.

The interpretation of Theorem 3 as 'as soon as the last layer is trained, the whole GNN is stationary' is somewhat stronger than the formal result. The theorem requires depth and a last-layer stationarity tolerance that can be exponentially small in L when alpha > 0, so the practical implication is less immediate than the prose suggests.

The spurious-stationary-point result is constructive but narrow: Corollary 2 uses centered regression and a very small last-layer norm, giving a high-loss near-stationary region but not convincingly showing that standard training commonly reaches such regions under realistic supervised node-classification setups.

The empirical evidence is only illustrative. Classification datasets are converted to regression with integer labels/MSE, all nodes are labeled, initialization is chosen to avoid vanishing signals, and there is no comparison to standard deep-GNN training recipes. This limits the evidential support for practical claims about why deep GNNs are hard to train.

Reproducibility details appear incomplete: the paper describes datasets and broad settings, but does not provide enough implementation detail, hyperparameters, random seeds, code availability, or precise training configurations to make the experiments readily reproducible.

The constants in the bounds can scale with graph size and stationary-distribution imbalance, and the practical magnitude of the bounds is not analyzed. This makes it hard to know when the theoretical conditions are meaningful for real graphs.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting optimization-side view of GNN oversmoothing via the backward signal, and the connection between backward smoothing, averaged output error, and near-stationarity is a potentially useful conceptual contribution.

The manuscript is mostly clear about the mathematical setup and distinguishes forward oversmoothing, backward oversmoothing, vanishing gradients, and stationary points. The comparison to MLPs is a useful attempt to show that the phenomenon is graph-specific.

The authors include full proofs in the appendix and discuss some scope limitations, especially that the analysis is for vanilla full-batch message-passing GNNs rather than skip connections, normalization, attention, or modern architectures.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overstated relative to the assumptions. The main results require forward oversmoothing as an assumption, smooth activations with Lipschitz derivative, full-batch training, irreducible stochastic propagation matrices, bounded spectral norms, sufficient depth, nonzero final forward signal, and stringent last-layer stationarity conditions. This is much narrower than the abstract and conclusion suggest.

The paper explicitly notes that forward oversmoothing is not proven for the important non-linear, non-symmetric stochastic case, yet the main theorem relies on it. This makes the claimed generality to non-linear and non-symmetric GNNs less convincing.

The empirical evidence is weak and mostly illustrative. Classification datasets are converted to regression with integer labels, all nodes are labeled, and the experiments use Leaky ReLU, whose derivative is not Lipschitz and is not covered by Assumption 5. Thus the experiments do not cleanly validate the stated theory or typical GNN training practice.

Reproducibility is limited: the appendix gives high-level settings but not enough detail on implementation, optimization hyperparameters, seeds, data splits, code availability, or exact procedures to reproduce the figures. Error bars are mostly absent despite stochastic initialization.

The practical significance is limited because the analysis excludes the main mechanisms used to train deep GNNs in practice, including residual/skip connections and normalization. The paper briefly discusses these only as future work, so it does not yet explain whether the phenomenon remains relevant for competitive architectures.

Some technical presentation issues reduce confidence: several claims such as 'as soon as the last layer is trained' are informal and stronger than the theorem statements; constants and rates are hidden in ways that may be unfavorable; and there are typographical or notation inconsistencies in proofs and figures.

The related-work positioning is plausible but somewhat aggressive, especially in criticizing prior work, while the present paper also leaves a key forward-oversmoothing gap unresolved and only gives qualitative numerical support.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful and underexplored optimization mechanism for deep GNNs: backward oversmoothing of the backpropagated error signal, and connects it to near-stationary points. This is a useful conceptual contribution beyond the standard forward-oversmoothing story.

The theoretical development is fairly substantial. The manuscript treats non-symmetric stochastic propagation matrices, distinguishes backward oversmoothing from ordinary vanishing gradients, proves that stationarity of the last layer can imply global near-stationarity under depth/expansion conditions, and includes an MLP counterexample to argue that the phenomenon is GNN-specific.

The exposition is generally clear and honest about scope. The authors explicitly state that they analyze vanilla full-batch GNNs rather than proposing a mitigation method, and they discuss why skip connections and normalization are left for future work.

The empirical figures, while illustrative, align with the theory: middle-layer backward oversmoothing is visible, deep GNNs quickly reach small gradients with high loss relative to MLPs on several real and synthetic datasets, and skip connections appear to mitigate the measured effect.
weaknesses: The main results rely on restrictive assumptions that substantially limit practical reach: fixed stochastic irreducible P, full-batch node-level gradients, bounded spectral expansion, smooth activations with Lipschitz derivative excluding standard ReLU, and a forward-oversmoothing assumption that is not proved for the important nonlinear, non-symmetric case. The authors acknowledge this gap, but it remains central because later results condition on it.

The empirical evidence is intentionally limited and not a convincing validation of the practical claim that this is the main reason deep GNNs are hard to train. Classification datasets are converted to integer regression with all nodes labelled, initialization is chosen near identity to isolate the phenomenon, and standard training setups, architectures, normalization, residuals, attention, and realistic semi-supervised splits are not evaluated.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives dataset names and broad settings, but I did not find code, detailed hyperparameters, optimizer settings, seeds, preprocessing details, or enough information to reproduce all plots exactly.

Some proof and presentation details need tightening. For example, the proof sketch around Theorem 3 appears to contain a notation/derivative typo when relating last-layer stationarity to the bound, and several constants/rate conditions are complex enough that clearer statements of regimes and dependencies would help readers assess when the results are non-vacuous.

The contribution is primarily explanatory rather than methodological. That is valuable, but the paper stops short of showing how the analysis leads to better optimization algorithms or to predictions that hold across common modern GNN variants. This limits significance despite the appealing idea.
Ethical issues appear minimal because the work is theoretical/diagnostic, but the manuscript does not include an explicit ethics or broader impacts discussion.
